generatedProse.concept-context: Across the School of Sport, an essay is expected to argue, not just describe. A question such as whether a training method improves performance wants a reasoned position, built from the evidence and shaped by the relevant literature. Different subjects build that position from different evidence: sport & exercise science leans on lab data and trials, coaching on practice-based judgement, management on policy and participation figures. The argument is carried by structure. The introduction states what you will argue, each body paragraph makes one point supported by sources, and the conclusion draws the case together.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two sport and exercise science students writing the introduction to an essay on the same question.

Tom opens with two broad sentences about why the topic matters, then lists what the essay will look at. It reads smoothly, but it never says what he will argue. His reader reaches the body with no sense of a position, so each study arrives as a separate point rather than a step in a case. This is structure without an argument.

Amara introduces the topic, notes briefly how the physiology literature tends to treat it, and ends with a clear line of argument: what she will argue, and why. Now her body has something to carry. Each paragraph makes one point that advances the argument, and the reader can follow the case building. This is structure doing its job.

Both introductions are well written. Only Amara used the structure to set up an argument the rest of the essay could carry.
generatedProse.summary: In the School of Sport, the argumentative essay is a continuous response built around one argument, and that argument is carried by structure. The introduction states the line of argument, the body makes one point per paragraph, and the conclusion synthesises them. Whether your evidence is lab data, a training record or a participation survey, the shape is the same. You can now recognise the argument in each part and say what a strong introduction must do. The next lesson shows how sources are woven in to support it.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's introduction stronger than Tom's?

items.text: It ended with a clear line of argument, so the body had a case to carry.
It was longer and used more technical sport science terms.
It listed everything the essay would look at.
It avoided mentioning the physiology literature.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara stated a line of argument, so each paragraph could advance it.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what let Amara's body build a case rather than offer separate points.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's introduction ended with a clear line of argument. Tom's listed topics and stated no case.
